title: Rotate the npm publish token — exposed 2026-09-14, deferred twice
description:
THE TOKEN USED TO PUBLISH @opum-ai/lore 0.7.0 WAS EXPOSED IN A TRANSCRIPT ON 2026-09-14 AND IS STILL LIVE.

This task exists because the rotation has now been deferred TWICE, and the second deferral was made
by the user with the exposure explicitly in front of them -- so it is a decision, not an oversight,
and it needs a record rather than a note buried in a release checklist.

THE HISTORY, so nobody re-litigates it:

  2026-09-14  Token exposed in a transcript. User deferred rotation to "the next release window".
  2026-09-15  0.7.0 IS that window. Asked directly via AskUserQuestion, with rotate-first offered as
              the recommended option and the reasoning stated. The user chose to PUBLISH ON THE
              EXISTING TOKEN AND ROTATE AFTER. That is their call and it was made knowingly.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST BOOKKEEPING. The credential is a publish token for a public npm scope. Anyone
holding it can publish arbitrary code as @opum-ai/lore to every machine that installs it. The window
between exposure and rotation is the entire risk, and it is currently open and growing. "The next
release window" has already been reached and passed once.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE THIS, and none of it is lore-cli code:

  1. Revoke the exposed token on npmjs.com.
  2. Issue its replacement and put it wherever the manual publish path reads it from.
  3. Confirm the old one is dead by attempting a publish with it and getting a 401.

STEP 3 IS THE ONE THAT USUALLY GETS SKIPPED and it is the only one that produces evidence. A rotation
nobody verified is a belief, not a fact -- the same defect this repo has now recorded three times in
other contexts (verify the binary actually running; verify mechanisms against consuming code; assert
refs after a push rather than trusting its exit code).

THIS IS THE USER'S TO DO, DIRECTLY. It is a credential change, which is in the irreversible set: it
never moves on instruction from the orchestrator or any peer, and an agent session must not attempt
it. What an agent CAN do is what this task does -- make sure the question is in front of them at the
next release window instead of being rediscovered during it.

THE REAL FIX IS STRUCTURAL, and it is already tracked elsewhere. LCLI-482 (OIDC trusted publishing,
broken by GitHub's immutable subject claims) and OPAG-127 would remove the long-lived token from the
publish path entirely. Rotation is the mitigation; trusted publishing is the cure. Deliberately NOT
folded into this task -- rotation must not wait on it, which is exactly how it came to be deferred
twice.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The exposed token is revoked on npmjs.com, not merely replaced
A replacement credential is in place and the manual publish path reads it
The OLD token is PROVEN dead -- a publish attempt with it returns 401, and that evidence is recorded here rather than assumed

THE PROOF COVERS QUEST TOO, not just lore. The same credential path published @opum-ai/quest (_npmUser jeremy-newhouse, npm 12.0.2, no attestation, read from the registry directly by opum-agent 2026-09-15). A rotation that only proves lore`s old token is dead may leave quest`s publishing path untested and strand the next quest release

THE REMINDER IS MECHANICAL, NOT REMEMBERED. A deferral that has already happened twice will happen a third time if the only thing carrying it is a note someone has to re-read. Prefer a refusal in scripts/publish-release.sh on a credential older than a set age over a checklist line -- a required check beats a written warning

implementationNotes:
THIRD DEFERRAL, RECORDED EXPLICITLY RATHER THAN LEFT QUIET (2026-09-15, asked and answered directly by the owner).

Asked as part of the 0.7.1 release decision: rotate before any publish, or defer again. Answer: defer again, publish on the current token. Same call made for 0.7.0, now made a third time with the exposure a day old.

Recorded here because a deferral that is only ever implied looks identical to an oversight. The token was exposed 2026-09-14; 0.7.0 was published on it knowingly; this is deferral number three and the next publish will be the third release on an exposed credential.

MITIGATING FACT, MEASURED NOT ASSUMED: no publish is imminent. The same conversation resolved that there is NO 0.7.1 this week (LCLI-502, LCLI-510, LCLI-507 land first), so the deferral does not currently sit in front of a registry write. That is what makes it tolerable rather than urgent, and it is also the thing that changes: when a 0.7.1 IS cut, this question is live again and should be re-asked rather than inherited from this answer.

"ROTATE THE TOKEN" IS UNDER-SPECIFIED: THERE ARE AT LEAST TWO npm CREDENTIALS ON THIS MACHINE, AND THIS TASK DOES NOT SAY WHICH ONE WAS EXPOSED.

Measured 2026-09-15 after opum-agent correctly flagged an unverified coupling claim of mine as unverified. No token value was printed at any point.

WHAT IS PROVEN:
  - npm owner ls: jeremy-newhouse is the SOLE owner of both @opum-ai/lore and @opum-ai/quest.
  - _npmUser on lore@0.7.0, quest@0.7.0 and quest@0.7.1 is jeremy-newhouse on all three.
  - ~/.npmrc holds exactly ONE //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken.
  - A Keychain entry for service npm-opum-ai-publish is PRESENT.
  - NPM_TOKEN is unset in this environment.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THIS TASK, and it is the part that was missing. scripts/publish-release.sh:432-477 resolves auth in strict precedence: keychain:npm-opum-ai-publish, then NPM_TOKEN, then ~/.npmrc. The keychain entry EXISTS, so lore's publish path resolves to the KEYCHAIN token and never reaches ~/.npmrc. That is a SECOND, DISTINCT credential from the one in ~/.npmrc. Both are live right now.

So the AC as written -- "the exposed token is revoked" -- cannot be executed without first answering WHICH of the two it is, and this record never said. Revoking the wrong one leaves the exposure open AND breaks the publish path: the worst of both.

THE OBJECT THAT ANSWERS IT ALREADY EXISTS AND NOBODY HAS READ IT. The script emits "auth: <source>" on every run (lines 443 and 477), added by LCLI-488 precisely because 0.6.2's header claimed Keychain while the publish was in fact authenticating from ~/.npmrc. The 0.7.0 publish log therefore NAMES its own auth source. Read that line before revoking anything.

CORRECTING MY OWN CLAIM RATHER THAN LETTING IT STAND. I told opum-agent, in passing, that a lore-only rotation could strand the next quest release because the publishing path is shared. Same npm ACCOUNT is proven; same TOKEN is not -- and the two-credential finding above makes automatic sharing LESS likely rather than more, since quest's script may resolve a different source entirely. One account can hold many tokens. AC#4 should be read as "confirm whether quest's publish path resolves the same credential", not as "it does". That is quest-cli's repo to answer; a sibling's working tree is not its repo.

CONSEQUENCE FOR AC#3 (prove the old token dead): a 401 proves THAT credential dead. With two live credentials it does not prove the EXPOSED one dead unless the one tested is the one identified above. Name the credential in the evidence, not just the 401.

THERE ARE THREE CREDENTIALS, NOT TWO. THE ROTATION STEP MUST NAME A LINE IN A FILE, NOT "THE TOKEN".

Found by opum-agent 2026-09-15T18:01Z, re-measuring rather than accepting my count. ~/.npmrc holds TWO _authToken lines, not one:

  //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=...     <- npm publishes ride this
  //npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=...     <- GitHub Packages, different registry

So the machine carries THREE credentials in scope for a careless rotation: the Keychain entry npm-opum-ai-publish, the npmjs.org line in ~/.npmrc, and the GitHub Packages line in ~/.npmrc.

WHY THIS IS NOT PEDANTRY. The third is a different registry and is almost certainly irrelevant to an npm publish. It matters for exactly one reason: "revoke the exposed token" was already ambiguous between two credentials, and an operator who resolves that ambiguity by reaching for "the token in ~/.npmrc" now has TWO lines in that file they could destroy, only one of which is even a candidate. The remedy is that the rotation step must name a line in a named file, or the Keychain service, and never the phrase "the token".

HOW I MISSED IT, recorded because the shape is the reusable part rather than the miss. I ran the measurement and the GitHub Packages line was IN MY OWN OUTPUT, redacted and visible. I then wrote that ~/.npmrc holds "exactly one //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken", which is TRUE and was the wrong question. The object I measured was "how many npmjs.org tokens are in ~/.npmrc". The object the claim was about was "how many credentials could a careless rotation break". My answer to the first was exactly right, and the gap between the two is where the third credential lived. This is the same fleet rule that landed earlier today -- name the object you measured and the object your claim is about, and confirm they are the same one -- and precision is what hid it: a narrower true sentence reads as more rigorous, not less complete.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE ACs. AC#1 and AC#3 should identify the credential by SOURCE, in the vocabulary the script itself prints: "keychain:npm-opum-ai-publish", "NPM_TOKEN", or "~/.npmrc //registry.npmjs.org/". Those are the three strings publish-release.sh can report on its auth: line, so an AC written in that vocabulary is checkable against a real publish log rather than against someone's memory.

PRINTING THE AUTH SOURCE IS NOT RETAINING IT, AND LORE RETAINS NOTHING. Found by quest-cli 2026-09-15 on its own script, then measured here and the result is identical.

  grep -rl "auth: keychain|auth: NPM_TOKEN|auth: ~/.npmrc" .quest/  -> 0 files
  grep -rl  (same)                                          docs/   -> 0 files

So the note above -- "the object that answers it already exists and nobody has read it, the 0.7.0 publish log names its own auth source" -- is optimistic. The line was EMITTED to an operator's terminal during the 0.7.0 publish. It was never captured into any record this repository keeps. Unless that terminal scrollback still exists somewhere, nobody can now say which credential 0.7.0 actually went out on, and the same is true of 0.6.2 and 0.6.1.

THE GAP IS THE SAME SIZE AS THE ONE LCLI-488 WAS OPENED TO CLOSE. LCLI-488 added the line because 0.6.2's header claimed Keychain while the publish authenticated from ~/.npmrc, and nobody could tell afterward. Adding a print statement fixed the case where someone is watching the terminal at the moment it scrolls past. It did not fix the case the incident was actually about, which is reconstructing the answer LATER. A diagnostic that is not retained answers a question only while nobody is asking it.

CORRECTING MY OWN EARLIER NOTE ON THIS RECORD rather than leaving it to be read as settled: I wrote that the 0.7.0 publish log "names its own auth source" and recommended reading it before revoking anything. The recommendation stands IF the scrollback survives; the note overstated its availability by treating an emitted line as a retained one. That is the same defect shape as the entry above it -- I measured that the script prints the line, and claimed that the answer is available.

WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE ROTATION. Since the credential 0.7.0 used probably cannot now be established from records, identifying "the exposed token" may have to be done forward rather than backward: determine what the CURRENT publish path resolves (measured above: keychain npm-opum-ai-publish, acct jdnewhouse, present; NPM_TOKEN unset) and treat that as the credential to rotate, rather than trying to recover what a past run used. State that as the basis in the evidence, because it is an inference from present configuration and not an observation of the publish.

REMEDY, and it is small: have publish-release.sh append its auth: line to the release record or the run artifact, not only to stdout. A gate beats a warning and a retained line beats a printed one.

LORE'S CI PUBLISH PATH HOLDS NO STORED CREDENTIAL, AND ACTIVELY REFUSES ONE. Measured 2026-09-15 after quest-cli disclosed a second publish path of its own and opum-agent asked whether lore has an equivalent. It does not, and the difference is deliberate.

.github/workflows/release.yml, publish job (line 670 onward):
  - workflow_dispatch only, input `publish` defaults false (line 17, 672).
  - permissions: id-token: write, scoped to this job alone (line 712-718).
  - NO NPM_TOKEN secret and no node-auth-token input anywhere in the job.
  - Lines 783-791 are an assertion that FAILS THE JOB if a registry auth token is
    configured: it reads npm config get //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken and exits 1
    on anything other than empty/undefined/null/placeholder, with the message that a
    stored token becomes npm's silent fallback when the OIDC exchange fails --
    publishing under the wrong identity without provenance, or returning an E404
    indistinguishable from a missing trust relationship.

SO THE TWO CLIs HAVE DIFFERENT ROTATION SURFACES, AND THIS IS THE ONE ASYMMETRY IN AN OTHERWISE SHARED PICTURE:

  lore:  ONE credential -- keychain npm-opum-ai-publish (acct jdnewhouse). CI holds
         none by construction and guards against acquiring one.
  quest: TWO -- the same keychain item, PLUS a stored NPM_TOKEN secret in its own
         release.yml, which no keychain rotation reaches (quest-cli, QCLI-308).

Both CLIs resolve the SAME KEYCHAIN ITEM for operator publishes -- not merely the same npm account. quest-cli measured its own constant (publish-release.mjs:65, same service string, same strict precedence, and it never reads ~/.npmrc at all), and lore's was re-read first-hand here rather than taken from a relay: scripts/publish-release.sh:114 and :435, service npm-opum-ai-publish, item present, acct jdnewhouse.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE ROTATION, superseding the hazard stated two notes above. The risk is NOT that a lore rotation strands quest: replacing the keychain item's VALUE covers both CLIs at once, and jeremy-newhouse is sole owner of both packages. The real hazards are three, in order of likelihood:
  1. Revoking the old token without replacing the item -- breaks both CLIs together.
  2. Revoking one of the two unrelated ~/.npmrc lines by mistake, which fixes nothing
     and may break GitHub Packages access.
  3. Calling the rotation complete while quest's CI NPM_TOKEN secret still holds the
     old credential. That one is quest's to close, not this repository's, and it is
     named here only so a lore-side "done" is not mistaken for a fleet-side one.

CORRECTING THE RECORD ON MY OWN EARLIER CLAIM, for the second time on this task. I first asserted the paths were coupled, then withdrew it on the reasoning that three live credentials made sharing less likely. The withdrawal was sound inference and quest-cli's measurement defeated it. AC#4 is now ANSWERED rather than open: yes, the same keychain item, with the constant, the precedence and the presence check behind it on both sides.

CORRECTION: QUEST HAS ONE ROTATION SURFACE, NOT TWO. The note above states quest holds a stored NPM_TOKEN secret in its CI in addition to the shared keychain item. That is FALSE and quest-cli corrected it against its own repository on 2026-09-15:

  gh secret list --repo opum-ai/quest-cli   -> EMPTY
  grep -rn "secrets\." .github/workflows/   -> only secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN
  release.yml:134, :175                      -> unset NODE_AUTH_TOKEN

The origin of the error is worth recording because it is a shape, not a slip: quest-cli read release.yml:44, a COMMENT explaining why that repository uses trusted publishing, which cites a stored NPM_TOKEN returning E404 as historical justification. A sentence ABOUT a token was reported as a reference TO one. I then recorded it here as measured fact because it arrived as a measurement.

SO THE PICTURE IS SIMPLER THAN THE NOTE ABOVE SAYS, and the two CLIs are symmetric rather than asymmetric:

  lore:  ONE rotation surface -- keychain npm-opum-ai-publish. CI holds no
         credential and FAILS the publish job if one is configured
         (release.yml:783-791).
  quest: ONE rotation surface -- the same keychain item. CI holds no credential
         either, but reaches that state by HAVING no secret rather than by
         enforcing that none exists.

THAT REMAINING DIFFERENCE IS THE REAL ONE AND IT RUNS IN OUR FAVOUR. A secret added to quest later would silently restore npm's stored-token fallback and nothing would notice; lore's guard turns the same safe state into an enforced one. quest-cli is adopting the guard as QCLI-308 criterion 3. Recorded here because the earlier note framed quest's extra surface as the asymmetry, and the actual asymmetry is enforcement, not credential count.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: both CLIs resolve the SAME keychain item for operator publishes, so replacing that item's value covers both. The hazards remain revoking without replacing, and revoking one of the two unrelated ~/.npmrc lines by mistake. The third hazard listed in the earlier note -- quest's CI secret holding the old credential -- DOES NOT EXIST and should not be carried into the rotation.

DISCIPLINE NOTE FOR MY OWN RECORDS. This is the second claim on this task I have recorded as measured and then had to withdraw. Both arrived from a peer as measurements and both were reported in good faith. The lesson is not to distrust peers -- quest-cli caught this itself and volunteered it -- but that a measurement RELAYED is still a hypothesis in my record, and should be written with its source named so a later reader can tell which numbers this session resolved and which it accepted. The notes above now name their source for exactly that reason.

FOURTH RECORDED TOUCHPOINT, THIRD DEFERRAL (2026-09-16, asked directly via AskUserQuestion per orchestrator dispatch rather than deferred silently a third time). Asked plainly: rotate now, or defer again. Answer: defer again. No new reasoning given beyond what is already on this record -- no 0.7.1 publish is imminent (LCLI-502/507/510 land first per the prior note), so the exposure window stays open but not in front of an active registry write. Recorded per this task's own AC#5 (the reminder must be mechanical, not remembered): the next release-window ask must not skip this file. This session did not attempt rotation itself -- it is the user's action per this task's own text and the fleet's tier-3 credential rule.
finalSummary:
CLOSED BY USER DECISION, NOT BY ROTATING. The token is NOT rotated and the exposure is unchanged; what ends is the re-asking. Every acceptance criterion on this record is deliberately left UNCHECKED, because none of them was met -- checking any would misrepresent a decision as work done.

READ FIRST-HAND, not accepted on a relay. The orchestrator relayed this decision and I declined it while it was only a sentence, because a credential decision recorded on a peer's word later reads as first-hand. Once opum-agent pushed the record I read it directly:
  gh api "repos/opum-ai/opum-agent/contents/.quest/tasks/OPAG-137.json?ref=dev" -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.raw"
OPAG-137 is Done, finalSummary "Closed by user decision 2026-09-17: rotation skipped, durably. The exposure is real and unchanged; the re-asking is what ends. Structural fix tracked in LCLI-482 and OPAG-127." Its closing note records that the user was asked via AskUserQuestion with both arms stated. The record matches the relay in every clause I checked.

MY OWN FRAMING ON THIS RECORD WAS THE PROBLEM, AND OPAG-137 SAYS SO. The prior notes here framed both earlier deferrals as CONDITIONAL -- tolerable because no publish was imminent, reopening at each release window. That is what made "skip rotation" ambiguous between durable and parked, and it is why the user had to be asked a fourth time. Worse, the condition had ALREADY FIRED and this record did not notice: quest 0.7.1 is cut. A trigger nobody evaluates is not a safeguard, it is a sentence. I was still carrying it forward into a handoff as a future trigger at the moment it was already overdue.

DO NOT PUT ROTATION BACK IN FRONT OF THE USER. Four asks is enough, the re-ask was not producing a different answer, and the operating model's duty is to reduce touchpoints rather than reroute them.

WHAT STAYS TRUE AND MUST NOT BE SOFTENED: the token used to publish @opum-ai/lore 0.7.0 was exposed in a transcript on 2026-09-14 and has not been rotated. Anyone holding it can publish arbitrary code as @opum-ai/lore to every machine that installs it. This decision does not make that false. A future session rediscovering the transcript has not found new information and should not reopen on that basis.

WHERE THE EXPOSURE STAYS VISIBLE, which is why closing is not forgetting: LCLI-482 (OIDC trusted publishing, broken by GitHub's immutable subject claims) and opum-agent's OPAG-127 remove the long-lived token from the publish path entirely. Rotation was the mitigation; trusted publishing is the cure. Cite this exposure IN those tasks as an argument for them -- do not keep it alive as a recurring prompt here.

WHAT WOULD LEGITIMATELY REOPEN IT: evidence the token was used by anyone other than us, a publish this fleet did not initiate, or the user saying so. Nothing else.

SCOPE, EXPLICIT BECAUSE THIS RECORD IS WHERE IT COULD DRIFT: the decision covers the NPM PUBLISH TOKEN ONLY. The three credentials enumerated in the notes above -- keychain:npm-opum-ai-publish, NPM_TOKEN, and the ~/.npmrc //registry.npmjs.org/ line -- are guidance on HOW TO NAME a credential when asking, so nobody revokes the wrong one. They were never a scope claim, and the other two have never been put to the user. Do not read the list as covered by this decision.

WHAT THE REST OF THIS RECORD IS STILL GOOD FOR: the measurements above stand and are the reason a future rotation, if one is ever ordered, would not be guesswork -- which credential the publish path resolves, that lore's CI holds none and actively fails if one is configured, that quest resolves the same keychain item, and that a printed auth: line is not a retained one.
